docs.title: Nebula Broadcast Automation & MAM
docs.text:
Nebula is a professional, open-source media asset management (MAM) and broadcast automation system engineered from the ground up for demanding, 24/7 broadcast environments.

It serves as the central orchestrator for media assets, scheduling, and playout control, offering broadcast operators a unified, lightning-fast workflow.

  • Getting Started

    Understand the architecture, main system services (Server, Worker, Services), and user interfaces.

    Learn Core Concepts · Tour the UI

  • Deployment

    Get Nebula up and running quickly using Docker Compose. Set up database, queue, server, and workers.

    View Installation Guide

  • Configuration

    Customize settings templates, register local/shared storage points, and set up watch folders.

    Settings System · Configure Storages

  • Playout Integration

    Integrate with CasparCG Server for high-performance graphic overlays, audio, and video playout.

    Playout Setup · Linear Rundowns

docs.title: What Nebula Can Do
docs.text: Everything below happens in one web interface, which updates live as colleagues and background services change things.

docs.title: Manage media
docs.text:
• Find anything fast: Browse the library in tabs, with thumbnails if you like, narrow it down with search and filters, and keep the combinations you use often as saved views.
  • Describe it your way: Folders give each kind of content (movies, episodes, commercials, jingles...) its own metadata form, and links between folders connect related assets, such as a series and its episodes.
  • Preview and trim in the browser: Play a proxy of any asset with frame accuracy, trim it, mark sub-clips and pick a poster frame, all from the keyboard if you like.
  • Transcription (coming soon): Automatic speech-to-text for your assets, so you can search what was said and select a passage straight from the transcript.

docs.title: Get media in
docs.text:
• Watch folders: Files dropped on a share become assets automatically, with their technical metadata filled in.
  • Upload and import: Upload from the browser or let the import service transcode incoming files to your house format.
  • Background jobs: Actions create proxies, transcode and deliver media without anyone clicking, and the jobs monitor shows their progress.

docs.title: Schedule and play out
docs.text:
• Plan the week: Lay out programme blocks in the scheduler calendar, by hand or from a scheduling template.
  • Build the rundown: Drag assets from the browser into the rundown. Use placeholders for media that has not arrived yet, add live events and lead-ins and lead-outs.
  • Go on air: Control the channel with the on-air controls, and decide per event and per item whether it starts automatically or waits for the operator.
  • Know what aired: Every played item lands in the as-run log.
  • Playout engines: Production playout runs on CasparCG. Conti, a lightweight software engine, is also available, but it is meant for testing only.

docs.title: Fit it to your station
docs.text:
• Configuration as code: Channels, folders, metadata fields and services are defined in settings files you can keep under version control.
  • Your own rules: Validators check and complete metadata whenever an asset is saved.
  • Scale out: Workers on several machines share transcoding, metadata extraction and playout control.
  • Open source and open API: Everything the interface does goes through a documented HTTP API, so other systems can do it too.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Understanding the core objects and architectural components of Nebula is key to designing efficient workflows and system integrations.

docs.title: Site
docs.text: A Site represents a single Nebula installation. A site can represent a broadcaster or a broadcast network with one or more channels sharing settings, users, and asset catalogs. * Each site has its own standalone database schema, configuration templates, and user access levels. * To distribute heavy workloads, a single site can run across multiple physical or virtual servers. * The backend foundation of a site consists of a PostgreSQL database, a Redis queue, and one or more shared storages.

docs.title: Server
docs.text: The Nebula Server provides the core Web API and serves the client-side user interface. * The server must have direct network access to the PostgreSQL database, the Redis message broker, and the low-res media storage used for proxy files and user uploads.

docs.title: Worker
docs.text: A Worker is a background manager daemon that spawns and controls Nebula Services (small, task-specific programs). * Services perform automated tasks such as technical metadata extraction, transcoding, watchfolder monitoring, and playout engine control. * Workers are highly scalable and can be distributed across different machines on your network, allowing media processing tasks (like rendering and transcoding) to scale out horizontally. * You can also develop custom, site-specific services to integrate specialized broadcast hardware or proprietary APIs.

docs.title: Asset
docs.text: An Asset is the primary database record in Nebula. It represents a single logical unit of media or metadata and can hold an unlimited number of metadata attributes, technical details, and associated physical media files.

docs.title: Folder
docs.text:
Assets sharing identical default properties and metadata fields belong to the same Folder. Examples include:

  • Movie: A feature-length, standalone film.
  • Episode: An individual episode belonging to a larger series.
  • Story: A short-form news item or package.
  • Song: A single music track or music video.
  • Fill: Short-form interstitial media (e.g., promotional clips) used to bridge programming gaps.
  • Trailer: A promotional teaser for movies or shows.
  • Jingle: A brief channel identifier or audio watermark.
  • Graphic: Still images and graphics (e.g. logos, lower thirds).
  • Commercial / Teleshopping: Paid advertisements (short-form or infomercial formats).
  • Dataset: A container for non-video files (such as XML schedule imports, CSV logs).
  • Incoming: The default temporary landing folder for newly detected, unclassified assets.
  • Serie: A parent virtual asset grouping multiple child episodes together.

Custom Folders

Although Nebula permits customization of folders, some default plugins and external automation integrations expect the default folders list to remain present.

docs.title: Content Type
docs.text:
The physical nature of an asset's data is defined by its Content Type:

  • AUDIO
  • VIDEO
  • IMAGE
  • TEXT
  • DATABROADCASTING
  • INTERSTITIAL
  • EDUCATION
  • APPLICATION
  • GAME
  • PACKAGE

docs.title: Media Type
docs.text:
An asset doesn't need to link to a physical media file. This is determined by its Media Type:

  • FILE: Represents a physical file on one of the registered storages.
  • URI: Points to an external stream or network URL.
  • VIRTUAL: Contains no physical media files; it acts purely as a metadata container (e.g. series metadata).

docs.title: View
docs.text: Views are customized asset filters used in the Nebula Browser. Each view configures which folders, asset statuses, and metadata columns (such as duration, date, or author) are displayed. Within a view, you can execute full-text searches and advanced queries.

docs.title: Actions & Jobs
docs.text:
• Action: A predefined, reusable process (e.g., "Transcode to MXF for Playout", "Archive to LTO Tape"). Actions define the conditions under which an asset can be processed.
  • Job: A specific execution of an action applied to an asset. Jobs can be triggered automatically (e.g., on watchfolder ingest) or manually.

docs.title: Channel
docs.text: A Channel represents a linear playout output. A single Nebula site can manage multiple playout channels concurrently. For installations dedicated solely to Video-on-Demand (VOD) or media archiving, Nebula can run without any channels.

docs.title: Event
docs.text: A calendar entry corresponding to an EPG block. An Event belongs to a channel and has a fixed start time and descriptive metadata (Title, Description, Category).

docs.title: Item
docs.text: An Item is an instance of an asset scheduled inside an Event rundown playlist. You can also insert special items that do not reference assets, such as live inputs, graphic overlays, or timing placeholders.

docs.title: Rundown
docs.text: A chronological list of all events and playlist items scheduled for a channel on a specific calendar day. The Rundown is the primary view used by broadcast operators to control and monitor the active playout.

docs.title: As-Run Log
docs.text: An automatic audit trail documenting the exact times that items were played. Nebula compiles this log for compliance reports, copyright auditing, and commercial billing exports.

docs.title: User Interface Overview
docs.text: The Nebula client interface provides access to the media catalog, metadata editor, background tasks monitor, and rundown scheduler.

docs.title: 1. Asset Browser
docs.text:
The Asset Browser is the primary catalog explorer for searching and organizing your media collection.

  • Tabs, Views and Filters: Keep several searches open in tabs, each with its own view, filters and columns. See Asset Browser for the details.
  • Asset Browser List: Displays assets matching the tab's view and filters. Clicking an asset opens it in the Asset Detail panel.
  • Context Menu: Right-clicking the selected assets offers:
    • Filter by the clicked column's value (adds a condition to the tab).
    • Send to...: start an action (e.g. a transcode or sending to playout) for the selection.
    • Reset: reload the assets' technical metadata from their files.
    • Archive and Trash.
  • Drag and Drop: Drag assets to the Scheduler to create events, or to the Rundown to add items.

docs.title: 2. Asset Detail Panel
docs.text:
The Asset Detail panel acts as the main metadata editor and proxy media player.

  • Metadata Fields: Allows users to view and edit metadata tags. The form updates dynamically based on the asset's assigned Folder (e.g., episode metadata fields differ from music video fields).
  • Offline Status: When a new asset record is created without a file (a "placeholder"), its status is set to Offline. You can manually assign an estimated duration to schedule it. Once the physical file is matched (e.g., via watchfolders or FTP naming conventions), the status changes to Online and Nebula updates the database record with the exact technical duration.

docs.title: 3. Jobs Monitor
docs.text: The Jobs page lists background jobs (transcoding, sending to playout...) in three views: Active, Finished and Failed. * Shows each job's asset, action, service, times and status message. * Pending and running jobs can be aborted, finished and failed ones restarted. * Clicking a job's priority cycles it through Hold, Lowest ... Highest; workers pick up higher-priority jobs first.

docs.title: 4. Scheduler
docs.text: The Scheduler shows a week of events for the selected channel. See Linear Broadcasting for the details. * Event Creation: Drag assets from the Browser into the calendar, or drag the Empty event icon from the toolbar. * Moving Events: Events have no fixed end time; drag them to a new start time. * Open Rundown: Double-click an event to open its day in the Rundown, scrolled to the event.

docs.title: 5. Rundown
docs.text: The Rundown is the item-by-item playlist of one channel's broadcast day. Three toggles in its toolbar add tools on top of the read-only view: Edit (change the rundown), Control (playout controls and on-air clock) and Plugins (playout plugins). See Linear Broadcasting.

docs.title: Docker-Based Installation
docs.text: This guide deploys Nebula with Docker Compose. The nebula-tutorial repository is a complete, working example of this setup: clone it and follow its README for a step-by-step walkthrough.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
A Docker deployment consists of four containers:

Service Image Role postgres postgres:18 Database: assets, events, settings, users, jobs redis redis:alpine Cache, sessions and the real-time message bus server nebulabroadcast/nebula-server Web interface and API (port 80 in the container) worker nebulabroadcast/nebula-worker Runs the services: watch folders, metadata, transcoding, playout control

More workers can run on other machines; each one starts the services assigned to its hostname (see Configuring Nebula).

docs.title: Directory Layout
docs.text:
nebula-tutorial/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── Makefile           # shortcuts: make setup, make reload, make update...
├── plugins/           # server and CLI plugins, mounted at /plugins
├── settings/          # settings templates, mounted at /settings
│   ├── actions.py
│   ├── channels.py
│   └── services.py
└── storage/           # media storage 1, mounted at /mnt/nebula_01

docs.title: Docker Compose Configuration
docs.text:
volumes:
  db: {}

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      - "POSTGRES_USER=nebula"
      - "POSTGRES_PASSWORD=nebula"
      - "POSTGRES_DB=nebula"
    volumes:
      - "/etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro"
      - "db:/var/lib/postgresql"
    restart: unless-stopped

  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    restart: unless-stopped

  server:
    image: nebulabroadcast/nebula-server:latest
    ports:
      - "4455:80"
    volumes:
      - "/etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro"
      - "./plugins:/plugins"
      - "./settings:/settings"
      - "./storage:/mnt/nebula_01"
    depends_on:
      - redis
      - postgres

  worker:
    image: nebulabroadcast/nebula-worker:latest
    hostname: worker
    volumes:
      - "/etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro"
      - "./storage:/mnt/nebula_01"
    privileged: true
    depends_on:
      - server
  • The worker's hostname matters: services are assigned to workers by hostname (host="worker" in services.py).
  • privileged: true lets the worker mount network storages itself (see Storages). A worker that only uses local storages doesn't need it.
  • A worker controlling CasparCG also needs its OSC ports published (see CasparCG Playout).

docs.title: First Start
docs.text:
docker compose up -d
make setup

make setup creates the database schema and applies the settings templates (see Configuring Nebula). The interface is then available at http://<host>:4455.

On an empty database, setup creates the user admin with the password nebula: change it right away with the built-in passwd command:

docker compose exec backend python -m cli passwd admin

More users are created in the web interface, or with adduser.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: make update pulls the latest images and recreates the server and worker containers. Release notes are on GitHub.

docs.title: CasparCG Playout
docs.text:
CasparCG Server is a professional-grade, open-source software available for both Windows and Linux, dedicated to playing out graphics, audio, and video to multiple outputs.

Nebula leverages CasparCG's stability and speed for real-time, on-air playout. Additionally, Nebula's playout control service supports custom plug-ins for secondary events (e.g., character generation, routers, studio switchers, recorders).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before configuring CasparCG playout, ensure: 1. CasparCG Server (v2.2 or later) is installed and running on a local machine or server. 2. A fast media drive is allocated for playout assets. 3. Network connectivity is open between the Nebula worker host and the CasparCG host.

docs.title: Controlling CasparCG from Docker
docs.text:
If your Nebula play service runs inside a Docker container, you must configure bi-directional communication between the service and the playout server: * Outbound control: Nebula commands CasparCG via AMCP protocol (TCP port 5250 by default). * Inbound feedback: CasparCG streams state feedback back to the Nebula worker via OSC protocol (UDP ports).

When running in Docker, you must expose the container UDP ports so CasparCG can connect and stream OSC feedback.

docs.title: 1. Configure the Playout Channel
docs.text:
In your site channel settings file (settings/channels.py), register a PlayoutChannelSettings entry with a unique controller_port and caspar_osc_port:

from nebula.settings.models import PlayoutChannelSettings, AcceptModel

# Define folder constraints for the calendar/rundowns
scheduler_accepts = AcceptModel(folders=[1, 2])
rundown_accepts = AcceptModel(folders=[1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10])

channel1 = PlayoutChannelSettings(
    id=1,
    name="Channel 1",
    fps=25.0,
    plugins=[],
    solvers=[],
    day_start=(7, 0),
    scheduler_accepts=scheduler_accepts,
    rundown_accepts=rundown_accepts,
    rundown_columns=[],
    send_action=2,
    engine="casparcg",
    allow_remote=False,
    controller_host="worker",
    controller_port=42101,
    playout_storage=3,
    playout_dir="media",
    playout_container="mxf",
    config={
        "caspar_host": "192.168.1.100",  # IP address of your CasparCG server
        "caspar_port": 5250,              # Default AMCP port
        "caspar_osc_port": 6251,          # Unique OSC feedback UDP port
        "caspar_channel": 1,
        "caspar_feed_layer": 10,
        "live_source": "DECKLINK 2",
    },
)

CHANNELS = [channel1]

docs.title: 2. Configure the Playout Service
docs.text:
In your settings/services.py, bind the channel ID to a playout service running on a specific worker:

from nebula.settings.models import ServiceSettings

PLAY1 = "<settings><id_channel>1</id_channel></settings>"

SERVICES = [
   ServiceSettings(id=11, type="play", name="play1", host="worker", settings=PLAY1),
]

docs.title: 3. Expose Ports in Docker Compose
docs.text:
In your docker-compose.yml, expose the UDP ports you specified in your channel config for the worker container:

services:
  worker:
    ports:
      - "6251:6251/udp"

docs.title: 4. Enable OSC in casparcg.config
docs.text:
On your CasparCG Server machine, open the casparcg.config configuration file and add the worker IP and OSC port to the predefined clients section:

<osc>
  <predefined-clients>
    <predefined-client>
      <address>IP_ADDRESS_OF_DOCKER_HOST</address>
      <port>6251</port>
    </predefined-client>
  </predefined-clients>
</osc>

docs.title: Media Directory Setup
docs.text:
Our recommended layout is to host a media.dir folder on the playout server's high-speed media drive (e.g. D:\media.dir on Windows). Share this folder on the network so it is accessible as a path (like \\playoutserver\playout).

In the server's casparcg.config file, set the <media-path> to point directly to your local media directory.

docs.title: Send-to-Playout Ingestion
docs.text:
To copy files automatically or manually from production storage to playout storage, configure a transcode/copy Action inside settings/actions.py:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<settings>
    <allow_if>True</allow_if>
    <task mode="ffmpeg">
        <param name="filter:a">"loudnorm=I=-23"</param>
        <param name="ar">48000</param>
        <param name="c:v">"copy"</param>
        <param name="c:a">"pcm_s16le"</param>
        <output storage="asset.get_playout_storage(1)" direct="1"><![CDATA[asset.get_playout_path(1)]]></output>
    </task>
</settings>

docs.title: Playout Storage Monitor (PSM)
docs.text: The PSM Service monitors the active playlist schedules and automatically queues transfer/transcode jobs to the playout server. * Timing: By default, it schedules files to transfer 24 hours before their scheduled broadcast time. * Scaling: Only one PSM instance is needed per site installation. It manages playout queues for all configured channels. No additional parameters are required.

docs.title: Live Sources
docs.text:
When a rundown block is set to LIVE, the playout controller instructs CasparCG to play the source defined under the channel's live_source configuration (e.g. a DeckLink physical input, a network NDI source, or an IP stream).

Changing Live Feeds

The live_source parameter is static and cannot be changed dynamically during a live show. If you need to switch between multiple inputs, either use an upstream hardware switcher (such as a Blackmagic ATEM) or route different video sources onto secondary CasparCG channels and command routing at the playout layer.

docs.title: Command Line Tools
docs.text: The backend has a command line interface for maintenance tasks. It runs inside the backend container and offers two kinds of commands: built-in ones that ship with Nebula, and site commands, which are your own CLI plugins.

docs.title: Running Commands
docs.text:
docker compose exec backend python -m cli              # list all commands
docker compose exec backend python -m cli <command>    # run one
docker compose exec backend python -m cli <command> --help

Without a command, the list of everything available is printed: built-in and site commands together, each with a one-line description.

A command that fails exits with status 1. A wrong command name or wrong arguments exit with status 2 and say what was expected.

docs.title: Built-in Commands
docs.text: Command What it does adduser Creates a user. passwd Sets a new password of a user. thumbnails Counts asset thumbnails, and makes the missing ones. version Prints the Nebula version.

docs.title: adduser
docs.text:
docker compose exec backend python -m cli adduser
docker compose exec backend python -m cli adduser jane --email jane@example.com --no-admin

Without arguments the command asks for the login, an optional e-mail, whether the user is an administrator, and the password (typed twice, not shown). Anything given on the command line isn't asked for. The e-mail is only asked for together with the login, so adduser jane --no-admin --password ... runs without stopping:

Argument Meaning login Login name. --email E-mail address. --full-name Full name. --admin / --no-admin Whether the user has administrator rights. --password The password. Prefer the prompt: a password on the command line ends up in the shell history.

The password must have at least 8 characters, and the login must not be taken. A user who isn't an administrator has no permissions until an administrator grants some in the web interface.

docs.title: passwd
docs.text:
docker compose exec backend python -m cli passwd jane

Sets a new password of an existing user, for example when they have forgotten it or the administrator account is locked out. The command asks for the login when it isn't given, and for the new password (typed twice, not shown) unless --password is given. The password must have at least 8 characters.

The user is logged out everywhere: every open session of theirs ends.

docs.title: thumbnails
docs.text:
docker compose exec backend python -m cli thumbnails status
docker compose exec backend python -m cli thumbnails sync
docker compose exec backend python -m cli thumbnails sync --limit 1000
  • status counts the assets that can have a thumbnail, and how many of theirs are ready, failed, stale (made for an older file, poster frame or marks) or missing.
  • sync makes the missing and stale thumbnails of online assets, newest assets first, one at a time. It can be stopped and started again. --limit stops after that many; --retry-failed also tries again the files that couldn't be read before.

Thumbnails are made anyway the first time someone looks at an asset, so sync is only needed to fill a library in advance.

docs.title: Site Commands
docs.text:
Site commands are Python files in the cli/ subdirectory of the backend's plugin directory (/plugins in the backend container, configurable with the NEBULA_PLUGIN_DIR environment variable):

plugins/
└── cli/
    ├── cleanup.py
    └── report.py

Each file defines a class based on nebula.plugins.CLIPlugin. Its name is the command name, and the class docstring is the description shown in the command list. The built-in commands are written the same way.

If two plugins have the same name, the first one found is used and a warning is printed. A site command with the name of a built-in command replaces it, also with a warning.

docs.title: A command
docs.text:
The plugin has an async def main method. Its parameters are the command's arguments:

import nebula


class Cleanup(nebula.plugins.CLIPlugin):
    """Remove old temporary assets."""

    name = "cleanup"

    async def main(self, folder: int, days: int = 30, dry: bool = False):
        ...

docker compose exec backend python -m cli cleanup 5 --days 7 --dry
  • A parameter without a default is a positional argument and must be given (folder).
  • A parameter with a default is an option: --days 7. A boolean is a flag: --dry, and --no-dry to turn it off.
  • Type hints give the types, so write them. typing.Annotated[..., typer.Option(help=...)] adds a description of an argument.
  • An underscore in a parameter name is a dash on the command line: retry_failed is --retry-failed.
  • The method's docstring, or the class's, is shown by --help, together with the arguments.
  • The settings are loaded before main runs, so nebula.settings and nebula.db are ready to use.

Note

Older versions took arguments as key=value (folder=5 dry=true). That form is no longer accepted: use --folder 5 --dry.

docs.title: A command with sub-commands
docs.text:
A plugin without main is a group. Every public async def method of the class is a sub-command, with arguments by the same rules:

import nebula


class Report(nebula.plugins.CLIPlugin):
    """Schedule reports."""

    name = "report"

    async def export(self, channel: int, days: int = 7, verbose: bool = False):
        """Export the schedule of a channel."""
        ...

    async def formats(self):
        """List the export formats."""
        ...

docker compose exec backend python -m cli report
docker compose exec backend python -m cli report export 1 --days 14 --verbose
docker compose exec backend python -m cli report formats

Methods whose names start with an underscore, and methods that aren't async def, are not commands: use them as helpers.

docs.title: Help texts and choices
docs.text:
The command line is built with Typer. A plugin doesn't need to import it, but can, to describe an argument further:

from typing import Annotated

import typer


async def main(
    self,
    days: Annotated[int, typer.Option(help="Age of the assets to remove.")] = 30,
):
    ...

Plugins written for earlier versions

They keep working without a change to their code, but they are called differently: --days 7 instead of days=7. Values now arrive converted to the type of the parameter's default (they used to arrive as text), so a check like if dry == "true" has to become if dry. A word that isn't one of the command's arguments is now an error (it used to be ignored).

docs.title: Configuring Nebula
docs.text:
Nebula's configuration is managed through a settings template, which is a set of Python modules that define various system, storage, and service parameters. This template allows you to customize Nebula's behavior to suit your specific broadcast requirements.

Settings templates are Python files in the settings/ directory of your deployment, mounted into the server container at /settings.

docs.title: Applying Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Whenever you modify settings templates, you must apply them to the system's database. With the nebula-tutorial setup, run make setup in its root directory, or call the commands it wraps directly:

makeDocker Compose 
make setup

docker compose exec server python -m setup
docker compose exec server ./manage reload

What does make setup do?

python -m setup loads the Python settings templates, validates them and stores the configuration in the PostgreSQL database. ./manage reload then reloads the server so it picks up the new settings. Workers read their settings when they start: restart them (make restart) after changing channels, services or actions.

docs.title: Configuration Files Map
docs.text:
Setup loads every .py file in /settings and looks for these variables. The file names are only a convention; one variable per file of the same name keeps things easy to find:

Variable Conventional file Purpose SETTINGS settings.py System settings (site name, proxy and upload storages, SSO providers, SMTP...) CHANNELS channels.py Playout channels STORAGES storages.py Storage volumes (local or Samba shares), see Storages SERVICES services.py Services and the worker (hostname) each one runs on ACTIONS actions.py Actions such as transcoding or sending to playout FOLDERS folders.py Asset folders and the fields shown in the metadata editor META_TYPES meta_types.py Metadata types (keys, classes, defaults) CS cs.py Additional classification schemes VIEWS views.py Views offered in the asset browser

Lists replace the defaults

SETTINGS and META_TYPES are dictionaries merged into the defaults, so they only need the keys you change or add. Every other variable is a list that replaces the built-in defaults as a whole: a FOLDERS list with one folder leaves the site with exactly one folder. Variables you don't define keep their defaults.

docs.title: Media Upload & Import
docs.text:
Watch folders create new assets from files. Media upload and import work the other way around: the asset already exists in Nebula (usually created by hand as an Offline placeholder), and a media file is delivered for it later.

Nebula supports two ways of doing that:

  • Direct upload: the file uploaded from the web interface is stored as the asset's media file as is.
  • Import: the file is handed to the import service, which transcodes it to your house format (for example XDCAM HD422) and then stores it as the asset's media file. The same service can also watch drop folders (e.g. FTP) for files named after an asset.

docs.title: Uploading from the Web Interface
docs.text:
When uploads are enabled, the asset editor shows an Upload button for existing file assets. Select a file and Nebula uploads it in the background; you can keep working and follow the progress in the upload monitor.

Nebula accepts the file only if:

  • the asset is a file asset (not a virtual one),
  • the file type matches the asset's content type (a video file for a video asset).

Uploads are enabled by default. To hide the button, set ui_asset_upload to False in the system settings (settings/settings.py):

SETTINGS = {
    "ui_asset_upload": False,
}

What happens to the uploaded file depends on whether an upload storage is configured.

docs.title: Direct Upload
docs.text:
Without an upload storage, the uploaded file replaces the asset's media file directly. No transcoding is done, so this mode fits setups where users deliver files already in the right format.

  1. The file is written to a temporary file on the asset's storage, then moved to the asset's path. If the file has a different extension than the asset path, the path is updated to match it.
  2. The asset status is set to Creating.
  3. The meta service probes the new file, updates technical metadata and turns the asset Online.

Note

The asset must already have a target storage and path. For assets created manually, these are assigned by the asset validator when the asset is first saved. Without them, uploads and imports for the asset fail.

docs.title: Upload Through the Import Service
docs.text:
To transcode uploads to your house format, configure an upload storage and directory in the system settings (settings/settings.py):

SETTINGS = {
    "upload_storage": 1,
    "upload_dir": "import",
    "upload_base_name": "{id}",
}
Setting Default Description upload_storage - Storage ID where uploaded files are placed. upload_dir - Directory on that storage where uploaded files are placed. upload_base_name {id} File name of the uploaded file (without extension). Formatted with the asset metadata, e.g. {id} or {id/main}.

An uploaded file is then saved as <upload_dir>/<upload_base_name>.<extension> (for example import/1234.mov), and the import service takes over.

You also need the import service and an import action, described below.

docs.title: The Import Service
docs.text:
The import service watches one or more import directories. For each file it finds, it:

  1. Waits until the file stops growing (its size must be the same on two consecutive checks).
  2. Finds the asset the file belongs to: the file name (without extension) must match the asset's metadata field set as identifier (by default the asset ID).
  3. Transcodes the file to the profile of the import action, into a temporary file.
  4. Moves the asset's current media file, if there is one, to a version backup (.nx/versions/ on the asset's storage), and moves the new file into its place.
  5. Moves the source file to the backup/ subdirectory of the import directory.
  6. Clears the asset's technical and QC metadata. The meta service then probes the new file and turns the asset Online, and jobs of the asset (for example proxy creation) are restarted.
flowchart LR
    U[Upload from web UI] --> D[Import directory]
    F[FTP / drop folder] --> D
    D -->|file matches an asset| T[Transcode to profile]
    T -->|success| A[Asset media file]
    T -->|failure| X["failed/ + error .txt"]
    A --> M[meta: Online]

Only video files are picked up.

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
Register a single instance of the service in settings/services.py:

from nebula.settings.models import ServiceSettings

SERVICES = [
    # ... other services
    ServiceSettings(id=6, type="import", name="import", host="worker"),
]

docs.title: Import Actions
docs.text:
Each import directory is configured as an action with the service type import (settings/actions.py). An action without id_storage and import_dir uses the upload storage and directory from the system settings, so for web uploads a minimal action is enough:

from nebula.settings.models import ActionSettings

import_settings = """
<settings>
    <profile>xdcamhd422-1080i50</profile>
</settings>
"""

ACTIONS = [
    # ... other actions
    ActionSettings(id=2, name="import", type="import", settings=import_settings),
]
Element Default Description id_storage upload_storage Storage ID of the import directory. import_dir upload_dir Directory on that storage to watch. Created automatically when the service starts. identifier id Asset metadata field the file name is matched against. profile xdcamhd422-1080i50 Target format, see Import Profiles.

Keep the file name and identifier in sync

For web uploads, upload_base_name must produce the value that identifier matches. The defaults ({id} and id) do. If you change one, for example to match on id/main, change both: upload_base_name = "{id/main}" and <identifier>id/main</identifier>.

The import service reads its actions when it starts. Restart the worker after changing them.

docs.title: Drop Folders
docs.text:
You can add more import actions, each watching its own directory, for example an FTP upload folder. Files dropped there must be named after the asset's identifier:

<settings>
    <id_storage>1</id_storage>
    <import_dir>ftp/incoming</import_dir>
    <identifier>id/main</identifier>
    <profile>xdcamhd422-1080i5994</profile>
</settings>

A file whose name matches no asset stays in the directory, and an error file with the same name and a .txt extension is written next to it (e.g. ABC123.txt for ABC123.mov). Once the media file is removed, the error file is cleaned up by the next import from that directory.

docs.title: Failed Imports
docs.text:
If an import fails (for example FFmpeg can't transcode the file, or the asset's file can't be written), the asset is left untouched: its current media file and status don't change. The source file is moved to the failed/ subdirectory of the import directory, together with a .txt file containing the error (for transcoding errors, the one reported by FFmpeg). The import job in the jobs list shows the first line of the error.

To retry, move the file from failed/ back to the import directory, or upload it again.

If the source file can't be moved out of the import directory at all, the reason is written to a .txt file next to it, and the file is skipped until it changes.

docs.title: Import Profiles
docs.text:
A profile defines the target format of an import. These profiles are included:

Profile Format xdcamhd422-1080i50 XDCAM HD422 1080i50 (PAL): MPEG-2 4:2:2, 50 Mbps, closed GOP 12, PCM audio xdcamhd422-1080i5994 XDCAM HD422 1080i59.94 (NTSC): MPEG-2 4:2:2, 50 Mbps, closed GOP 15, PCM audio

Both are meant for .mxf asset paths and output 1920×1080. Sources of another size (4K, 720p, SD, anamorphic HDV...) are scaled to fit, keeping their display aspect ratio, and padded with black bars where the aspect differs (a 4:3 source is pillarboxed).

docs.title: Fast Import
docs.text: If the source video already matches the profile (for example an XDCAM HD422 1080i50 file imported with the xdcamhd422-1080i50 profile), the video stream is copied instead of re-encoded. Only the audio is converted. This makes importing files that are already in the house format nearly instant.

docs.title: Profile Files
docs.text:
Each profile is a TOML file in the worker's services/import/profiles/ directory, named after the profile (<name>.toml). The profiles are loaded when the import service starts; an action that uses an unknown profile is skipped and an error is logged.

# "smca": merge several mono audio tracks into one multichannel track
audio_layout = "smca"

# Output frame size (square pixels). Other sizes are scaled to fit and
# padded. Leave out to keep the source size.
width = 1920
height = 1080

# FFmpeg video options for transcoding
video_encoding = [
    "-r", "25",
    "-pix_fmt", "yuv422p",
    "-c:v", "mpeg2video",
    # ...
    "-b:v", "50M",
]

# FFmpeg video options for a fast import (default: ["-c:v", "copy"])
video_copy = ["-c:v", "copy", "-b:v", "50M"]

# FFmpeg audio options
audio_encoding = ["-ar", "48000", "-c:a", "pcm_s16le"]

# Sources matching all keys of any entry use fast import.
# Keys: commercial_name, width, height, fps, aspect
[[video_fast_import]]
commercial_name = "XDCAM HD422"
fps = 25
width = 1920
height = 1080

Current limitations

  • Fast import doesn't check the scan type, so a progressive 1080p25 XDCAM file matches the 1080i50 profile and is copied as is.
  • Audio and image files are not imported.

docs.title: Uploading via the API
docs.text:
The web interface uploads files with a single HTTP request, which you can also use from your own tools:

curl -X POST "https://nebula.example.com/upload/1234" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    -H "X-nebula-extension: mov" \
    --data-binary @clip.mov

The asset ID is part of the URL, the request body is the file itself, and the X-nebula-extension header gives its file extension. The file then goes through direct upload or the import service, as configured above.

docs.title: Nebula Storages
docs.text: In a professional broadcast workflow, dividing high-capacity raw media from low-latency playout media is essential. Nebula separates these into distinct storage roles.

docs.title: 1. Production Storage
docs.text:
• Characteristics: High capacity for raw footage, high-res masters, and intermediate assets. It demands good concurrent I/O performance to handle ingest and transcoding but can tolerate higher access latency than playout.
  • Implementation: Network Attached Storage (NAS) or Storage Area Network (SAN) solutions are commonly employed, supporting standard protocols like NFS or SMB/CIFS. A hybrid array (SSDs for current projects, spinning disks for archival) provides the best balance of cost and performance.

docs.title: 2. Playout Storage
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Extremely high, consistent read performance with minimal latency. It only needs to hold media files for the active scheduling window (typically a few days or weeks).
  • Implementation: Direct Attached Storage (DAS) using high-speed SSDs (RAID 10) directly connected to the CasparCG playout server is the preferred standard.

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature Production Storage Playout Storage Purpose File ingest, editing, archiving, high-res masters Real-time playout, optimized delivery Capacity Large (terabytes to petabytes) Sufficient for active playout schedule (days/weeks) Performance High I/O for ingest/transcoding, moderate latency High read speeds, very low latency, consistent throughput Access Random read/write, large file transfers Sequential read, concurrent access by playout engines Redundancy High (RAID 6, distributed storage, backups) High (RAID 10, mirrored, fast failover) Connectivity SAN, NAS (NFS, SMB), Cloud Storage Direct Attached Storage (DAS), high-speed SAN/NAS File Formats Original camera formats, mezzanine codecs Playout-specific codecs (e.g., ProRes, DNxHD, H.264)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Storages in Nebula are referenced by their ID (e.g. 1, 2). Nebula expects storages to be mounted at /mnt/{site_name}_{id} on each system node (e.g. /mnt/nebula_01).

Storages use one of two protocols:

  • local: the directory is already there (a host folder bind-mounted into the containers, or a share the host mounts itself, e.g. NFS).
  • samba: the worker mounts the SMB/CIFS share at /mnt/{site_name}_{id} itself and remounts it when it drops.

All media assets are referenced inside the database by their storage ID and relative file path.

docs.title: Local Storage
docs.text:
On a single machine, bind-mount a host folder into both the server and the worker container. A storage that isn't listed in STORAGES is treated as local, so this needs no settings at all:

services:
  server:
    volumes:
      - ./nebula-storage:/mnt/nebula_01

  worker:
    volumes:
      - ./nebula-storage:/mnt/nebula_01

docs.title: Shared Network Storage (Samba)
docs.text:
To have the worker mount an SMB/CIFS share, define it in settings/storages.py:

from nebula.settings.models import StorageSettings

STORAGES = [
    StorageSettings(
        id=1,
        name="production",
        protocol="samba",
        path="//server/share",
        options={
            "login": "user",
            "password": "password",
        },
    )
]

After modifying the file, run make setup (or docker equivalent) to save this storage configuration to the database.

Docker Permissions for Network Mounts

Mounting network drives directly inside Docker containers requires administrative capabilities. The containers running the mounting tasks (such as nebula-worker) must be configured with privileged: true or the SYS_ADMIN capability.

Add this to your docker-compose.yml service configuration: 

privileged: true
cap_add:
  - SYS_ADMIN
  - DAC_READ_SEARCH

docs.title: Thumbnails
docs.text: Nebula shows a small picture of each video and image asset at the start of its title, in the asset browser and in the rundown. The server makes these thumbnails itself, the first time an asset's picture is asked for. There is nothing to set up or run.

docs.title: What a Thumbnail Shows
docs.text:
A thumbnail is a 320 pixels wide WebP picture of one frame:

  • the asset's poster frame, when one is set;
  • otherwise the frame 15 % into the asset, counted between its IN and OUT marks.

An image asset's thumbnail is the image itself, scaled down.

Only assets with a media file whose content type is video or image have thumbnails. Audio, text and virtual assets show a placeholder.

The picture is always made from the asset's own media file, never from its proxy: proxies may carry burn-ins such as a timecode or a logo.

docs.title: When a Thumbnail Is Made Again
docs.text:
A thumbnail belongs to the file and the frame it was made from. When the file changes (a new upload or import), or someone moves the poster frame or the marks, the old thumbnail is out of date and the next time the asset is shown a new one is made. Changing the metadata, such as the title, doesn't touch the thumbnail.

  • Offline files: making a thumbnail needs the media file. While the file is offline (an unmounted storage, archived media), the last thumbnail made is shown, even if it is out of date. A new one is made once the file is back. An offline asset that never had a thumbnail shows the placeholder.
  • Files that can't be read: when a file can't be read, the asset shows the placeholder, and the file isn't tried again until it changes (or thumbnails sync --retry-failed is run).
  • Many at once: each backend server makes one thumbnail at a time and shows the most recently requested ones first, so scrolling quickly through a large library doesn't queue thousands of them. Pictures that aren't ready yet show the placeholder for a moment.

docs.title: Storage and Backups
docs.text:
Thumbnails are kept in the database (the thumbnails table), not on a storage, so they can't go out of date or be left behind unnoticed: a thumbnail is deleted together with its asset. Each one takes a few kilobytes, so a library of half a million assets needs some gigabytes.

They can always be made again, so database backups can leave them out:

pg_dump --exclude-table-data=thumbnails nebula > nebula.sql

After a restore without them, thumbnails are made again as assets are viewed, or all at once with thumbnails sync.

docs.title: Asset Validators
docs.text: A validator is a site-specific Python plugin that runs every time an object is created or updated through the API, for example when a user saves an asset in the web interface. It is the place for your own rules: required fields, values derived from other fields, and where an asset's media file should live.

docs.title: Why You Need an Asset Validator
docs.text:
When an asset is created by a watch folder, its file already exists, so Nebula knows the storage and path. When a user creates an asset manually (an Offline placeholder waiting for its media), Nebula has no file to take them from.

The asset validator is responsible for setting the asset's storage (id_storage) and path (path) when the asset is first saved. They tell Nebula where the media file will be expected:

  • media upload stores the uploaded file there,
  • the import service writes the transcoded file there,
  • the meta service turns the asset Online when a file appears there (for example copied by hand).

An asset without a storage and path can't receive media: uploads and imports for it fail.

Don't overwrite an existing path

Only set the path if the asset doesn't have one yet. Assets created by watch folders already point to their file, and the path of an asset with media must not change on a later save.

docs.title: Where Validators Live
docs.text:
Validators are Python files in the validator/ subdirectory of the backend's plugin directory (/plugins in the backend container, configurable with the NEBULA_PLUGIN_DIR environment variable). There is one file per object type:

plugins/
└── validator/
    ├── asset.py
    ├── item.py
    ├── bin.py
    ├── event.py
    └── user.py

All files are optional. An object type without a validator is saved as sent.

Validators are loaded once, on first use. Restart the backend after changing a validator.

docs.title: Writing a Validator
docs.text:
A validator file defines an async validate function:

async def validate(
    asset: nebula.Asset,  # The existing asset, or a new empty one
    meta: dict[str, Any],  # Metadata sent in the request
    connection: nebula.DB,  # Database connection (kept for compatibility)
    user: nebula.User,  # User who made the request
) -> None:
    ...

Things to keep in mind:

  • Apply the request yourself. With a validator in place, Nebula doesn't copy the request metadata to the object; call asset.update(meta) (usually first) and then adjust what you need.
  • Don't save at the end. Nebula saves the object after validate returns. Call await asset.save() inside the validator only when you need the ID of a new asset, e.g. to build a path from it.
  • Reject with an exception. The validator runs in a database transaction. Raising ValidationException aborts the whole operation (nothing is saved, including an asset you saved inside the validator) and shows the message to the user.
  • Validators run for API requests only. Changes made by the worker, such as assets created by watch folders or metadata updated by the meta service, don't go through validators.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This validator requires a title, gives new assets a main identifier, and assigns the storage and path where the media file is expected:

from typing import Any

import nebula
from nebula.enum import ContentType, MediaType, ObjectStatus
from nebula.exceptions import ValidationException


async def validate(
    asset: nebula.Asset,
    meta: dict[str, Any],
    connection: nebula.DB,
    user: nebula.User,
) -> None:
    asset.update(meta)

    if not asset["title"]:
        raise ValidationException("Title is required")

    # A new asset needs an ID before we can build its path from it.
    # This happens inside the transaction, so a later exception
    # still rolls it back.
    if not asset.id:
        await asset.save()

    if not asset["id/main"]:
        asset["id/main"] = f"{asset.id:06x}"

    asset["media_type"] = MediaType.FILE
    asset["content_type"] = ContentType.VIDEO

    # Where the media file will be expected. Never change the path
    # of an asset that already has one (e.g. from a watch folder).
    if not asset["path"]:
        asset["id_storage"] = 1
        asset["path"] = f"media.dir/{asset['id/main']}.mxf"
        asset["status"] = ObjectStatus.OFFLINE

The file extension of the path should match the format your media arrives in. With the import service, use the container of the import profile (.mxf for the XDCAM profiles). With direct upload, the extension is updated to match the uploaded file.

Organising the storage

The path is built in Python, so it can use any asset metadata, for example a subdirectory per folder. Keep the paths unique, ideally based on an identifier that never changes.

docs.title: Watch Folders
docs.text:
Using watch folders is the most convenient way to automate media file ingestion in Nebula.

Watch folders monitor specific storage directories and automatically create corresponding database assets in Nebula as soon as new files are detected. This eliminates the need for manual asset creation and ensures that your media library is always up-to-date.

To enable watch folders, you must configure and run a single instance of the watch service in your setup.

docs.title: Minimal Configuration
docs.text:
In settings/services.py, add a service of type watch whose settings list the watched directories.

For each new file, an asset is created in the folder given by id_folder (by default Incoming):

<service>
    <folder id_storage="1" path="media.dir/movies" id_folder="1"/>
    <folder id_storage="1" path="media.dir/episodes" id_folder="2"/>
</service>

Register it with the XML as its settings:

from nebula.settings.models import ServiceSettings

WATCH = """
<service>
    <folder id_storage="1" path="media.dir/movies" id_folder="1"/>
</service>
"""

SERVICES = [
    ServiceSettings(id=2, type="watch", name="watch", host="worker", settings=WATCH),
    # ... the other services
]

docs.title: Customizing Folder Behavior
docs.text:
You can customize how files are scanned, matched, and processed using XML attributes within the <folder> tag:

Attribute Required Default Description id_storage yes - ID of the storage to watch. path yes - Directory to watch, relative to the storage root. id_folder no 12 Folder new assets are created in (12 is Incoming in the default folders). recursive no off Watch subdirectories too. hidden no off Also pick up hidden files and directories (names starting with a dot).

recursive and hidden take TRUE/FALSE (also 1/0, yes/no; case doesn't matter).

Older worker images

nebula-worker 6.1.0 and older turn these attributes on with any value, recursive="FALSE" included. On those, leave the attribute out to keep it off.

Files still being written

A new asset is created as soon as its file appears, even while it is still being copied (e.g. over FTP). Its status stays Creating until the file hasn't changed for 15 seconds; only then does the meta service turn it Online. The former quarantine_time attribute is no longer used and is ignored.

docs.title: Advanced Python Post-Processing
docs.text:
For complex workflows, you can write inline Python scripts inside a <post> block to programmatically inspect the file, extract sidecar metadata, or generate custom identifiers.

The newly created asset is exposed to the script via the asset variable.

docs.title: Example: Generating a Custom Identifier
docs.text:
This script runs after a file is matched. It uses the shortuuid library to set a unique key in the asset's main identifier:

<service>
  <folder id_storage="1" path="media.dir" recursive="TRUE" id_folder="1">
    <post>
<![CDATA[
import shortuuid
asset["id/main"] = shortuuid.uuid()
]]>
    </post>
  </folder>
</service>

Script Execution Sandbox

Post-processing scripts run with the privileges of the Nebula worker process. Ensure you only execute verified scripts to avoid security risks.

docs.title: Asset Browser
docs.text:
The Asset Browser on the left of the MAM pages is where you find assets: to open them in the editor, drag them to the rundown or the scheduler, or act on many at once. It works with tabs, like a web browser, so you can keep several searches open and switch between them without losing your place.

From the top: the tabs (with + for a new one), the filter bar (with ⟳ to reload), and the assets. The asset you click opens in the editor on the right.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Each tab is its own browser: it has a view, its own filters, search, sort, columns and thumbnails setting, and remembers its scroll position and which rows are selected.

  • New tab: the + at the right end of the tab bar. The new tab starts with the view of the tab you were in, as the view defines it (without the filters you added).
  • Close a tab: the × on the tab, or a middle click. The last tab can't be closed.
  • Switching tabs is instant. Nothing is reloaded, and you come back to the same rows at the same scroll position.
  • The tab label is the view's name, followed by the search, if there is one.

Your tabs (views, filters, searches, sorts, columns and thumbnails) are restored when you reload the page. Rows, scroll positions and selections are not.

Tabs and your own views live in the web browser

They are stored in the web browser you use, not on the server. Another computer, another web browser or a private window starts with one tab of the first view, and none of your own views. On a shared computer, everyone who logs in with the same web browser shares the same tabs and views.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a starting point for a tab: which assets it shows, which columns, and in what order. Click the filter bar to open the popover; the views are in its left column.

  • Views are the site's views, set up by the administrator (views.py, see Settings System). Typically one per kind of content: movies, episodes, commercials, trash...
  • My views are the ones you saved yourself.

Picking a view replaces the tab's filters, search, sort and columns with the view's. The view's folders and statuses become ordinary filters (Folder is any of ..., Status is any of ...), so you can change or remove them like any other.

When the tab's filters or search differ from its view, the filter bar shows a × ("Back to the view's filters") that returns to them.

docs.title: Saving your own views
docs.text:
When a tab shows something you'll want again, save it:

  • Save as new view... at the bottom of the view list: give it a name. It keeps everything the tab shows: filters, search, sort, columns, column widths and thumbnails. The tab then shows the new view.
  • Save changes to <view> appears when the tab shows one of your views and you've changed something in it.
  • Rename (pencil) and delete (bin) are next to each of your views.

Your views are stored in your web browser, like your tabs (see the note above): they can't be shared with colleagues on other computers.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Type into the filter bar and press Enter.

  • Every word must match. A word matches the beginning of words in the asset's metadata, so galax guard finds Guardians of the Galaxy.
  • Case and accents don't matter.
  • Words shorter than three letters are ignored.
  • Only the fields the administrator marked as searchable are searched. By default these are titles, subtitles, descriptions, keywords, notes, IDs, people (director, cast...) and the file path. To look in a specific field, use a filter instead.

To clear the search, delete the text and press Enter.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filters narrow the tab to assets whose fields have certain values: "Genre is any of Drama", "Duration > 01:00:00", "Director is set". A tab shows the assets that match all its filters (and the search).

Click the filter bar to open the popover. In Filters mode (the default) it lists the tab's filters, and below them the fields you can filter by.

Here the tab shows the Main view, whose folders became the first filter. A second filter keeps films directed by Ridley Scott, and alien typed in the bar is offered as the search.

docs.title: Adding a filter
docs.text:
1. Click a field in the list, or start typing its name in the filter bar to find it (the name or its key, e.g. genre).
  2. Pick an operator and fill in the value.
  3. Click Add filter, or press Enter.

Two shortcuts:

  • field:value typed in the filter bar adds the filter "field is value" when you press Enter. For example genre:drama title words filters by genre and searches for the rest. Use the field's key, as the field list shows it in grey.
  • Filter by <field> in the context menu of a cell (right click) filters by that cell's value. It replaces an existing filter on the same field.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Which operators a field offers depends on its kind:

Field Operators Text contains, is, is not Numbers, dates, durations is, is not, <, ≤, >, ≥ Fixed values (folders, statuses, classifications) is, is not, is any of, is none of (only the last two for hierarchical classifications) Lists (several values in one field) contains Yes/no is

Most fields also have is set and is not set, for assets where the field has, or hasn't got, any value.

Fields with a fixed set of values offer them to pick from, with a search for long lists. In hierarchical classifications, such as genres with sub-genres, values are shown as a tree, and picking a value includes everything under it: Drama also finds Crime drama.

docs.title: Changing and removing filters
docs.text:
• Click a filter to edit it.
  • The × on a filter removes it; clear all removes them all.

Every change reloads the tab.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
In the popover, switch to Columns:

  • Reorder columns by dragging them in the list.
  • Hide a column with its ×. The title column can't be hidden: it names the asset.
  • Add a column by clicking a field below the list (type in the filter bar to find it).

Columns, like filters, belong to the tab, until you pick another view. Save the tab as your own view to keep them.

docs.title: Thumbnails
docs.text:
Show thumbnails, at the top of the Columns panel, puts a small picture of each asset at the start of its title. It is off in the site's views; turn it on in a tab, and save the tab as your own view to keep it on.

The picture is the asset's poster frame, or a frame near its beginning. Assets without a picture (audio, text, virtual assets, or a file that can't be read) show a placeholder, and so does an asset whose picture is still being made. See Thumbnails for how they are made.

Widths: drag the right edge of a column header to resize it, double-click the edge to return to the automatic width. Widths are remembered per view, so every tab with that view uses them. The last column fills the rest and can't be resized.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Click a column header to sort by it, click again to reverse. New tabs show the newest assets first.

The Duration column sorts by the duration as it is shown: between the IN and OUT marks when the asset is trimmed.

Not every field can be sorted by: sorting needs a database index, which the administrator sets up for the fields that need one. When a field can't be sorted, a message says so, the tab keeps its order, and the header stops being clickable.

docs.title: Scrolling and updates
docs.text:
There are no pages: scroll down and more assets load as you go.

The browser keeps up with changes as they happen, in every tab, including the ones you're not looking at:

  • A changed asset is updated in place. It doesn't move, even when the change affects the sort (a renamed asset stays where it was until you reload).
  • An asset that no longer belongs in the tab (moved to another folder, trashed...) disappears from it.
  • New assets appear at the top of tabs sorted by newest first. Other tabs show N new on the tab: click it to reload.

The ⟳ button next to the filter bar reloads the tab.

docs.title: Selecting and acting on assets
docs.text:
• Click an asset to select it and open it in the editor.
  • Ctrl+click adds or removes an asset from the selection; Shift+click selects a range.
  • ↑ / ↓ move to the previous or next asset.

Each tab has its own selection, but there is only one editor: it shows the asset you last clicked, and switching tabs doesn't change it.

Actions work on the selection of the tab you're in, so only on assets you can see:

  • Drag assets to the rundown or the scheduler.
  • Right click for the context menu: Send to..., Reset, Archive, Trash, and Filter by the clicked cell.

docs.title: Links between folders
docs.text: Folders can be linked: an episode to its series, for example. The asset editor then offers the link in its menu (e.g. Show episodes), which opens a new tab with the linked view and a filter for the current asset.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
In the filter bar:

Key Does typing searches, and narrows the field list ↑ / ↓ move through filters, fields and views Enter picks the highlighted row, or searches Esc closes the filter being edited, then the popover

In the list of assets, ↑ / ↓ move to the previous or next asset.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
The scheduler shows a week of events of the selected channel.

The quickest way to schedule is to drag an asset from the browser into the calendar. A new event is created at the drop position, with the asset's title and description, and the asset becomes the event's first item. Which folders can be dropped is set per channel (scheduler_accepts).

To create an empty event, drag the Empty event icon from the scheduler toolbar into the calendar; a dialog asks for its metadata.

Events have no fixed end time: an event lasts until the next one starts. Drag an event to move it, or change its start time with Edit in its context menu. Delete removes it.

Holding Ctrl while dropping an episode of a series opens Schedule series: the following episodes are scheduled into a recurring slot (daily or weekly on chosen days, until a date or for a number of episodes).

The toolbar also has Apply template, which fills the week from a scheduling template (if the channel has any), and Delete unaired, which removes the week's events that haven't been broadcast yet.

Double-click an event to open its day in the rundown, scrolled to the event.

Editing the schedule requires the scheduler_edit permission for the channel.

docs.title: Rundown
docs.text:
The rundown is the item-by-item playlist of one broadcast day. With all toggles off, it shows the day's events and items with their scheduled times. Three toggles in the toolbar add tools; they can be combined, and each is offered only to users with the permission for the current channel:

Toggle Adds Permission Edit Dragging assets from the browser into events, reordering items, the special items toolbar rundown_edit Control On-air controls with the clock and progress, cueing by double-click mcr Plugins The channel's playout plugins mcr

The toggles are remembered in the browser. Items and events can also be changed from their context menu (edit, run mode, delete).

Every item shows a small picture of its asset before the title (a placeholder for items without one, such as live events); see Thumbnails.

docs.title: On-air controls
docs.text:
Since video servers take time to load a video file for playout, Nebula always loads the next clip while playing the current one. The clip currently playing is highlighted red, the next one (cued) green. With Control on, double-clicking an item cues it; it starts when the current one finishes.

The on-air panel shows the current and the cued item with their remaining times, and these buttons:

  • Take plays the cued item now
  • Freeze pauses or resumes the current clip
  • Retake replays the current item from the beginning
  • Abort stops the current clip and pauses on the first frame of the cued one
  • Cue prev / Cue next cue the previous or next item

By default, the application plays items one after another, but this behavior can be changed to create loops within the blocks, wait conditions and so on using run modes both for events and items.

docs.title: Event run modes
docs.text:
• Auto: Playback of the block starts right after the last clip of the previous block is finished.
  • Manual: The previous block plays in a loop until an item from this block is manually cued.
  • Soft: The previous block plays in a loop until the start time of this block is reached. After that, the first item of the block is cued, and starts when the currently playing clip is finished.
  • Hard: Similar to the soft mode, but when the event start time is reached, hard cut is used instead waiting for the current clip to be finished.

docs.title: Item run modes
docs.text:
• Auto: Playback starts automatically right after the last clip is finished.
  • Manual: The previous item stops at its last frame until take or abort button is pressed to advance to the next item.
  • Skip: The item won't be played and its duration is not accounted to the rundown computed time. This mode is useful for scheduling "backup" clips for the case live event ends earlier than expected.

docs.title: Special items
docs.text: With Edit on, a toolbar with these special items appears; drag them into the rundown:

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text: A placeholder reserves time for content that isn't known yet. If the channel has solvers configured, Solve using ... in the placeholder's context menu replaces it with real items.

docs.title: Live events
docs.text: When playback reaches the live event, the playout server is switched to its configured live source (for example the feed from the studio).

docs.title: Lead in/out
docs.text: Special markers to be used in looped blocks. Lead-in marks the point, where the playback continues after reaching the end of the loop, lead-out marks the end of the looped part.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: When the run mode of the next block is set to soft, the part before lead-in marker is played, then the part between both markers plays in the loop and when the start time of the next block is reached, the current clip finishes, then the part after the lead-out marker is played and finally, the next block starts.

docs.title: Video Preview & Trimming
docs.text: The video preview player provides the asset detail interface with tools to view low-resolution proxies, define poster frames, trim clips, and generate sub-clips.

docs.title: Poster Frame
docs.text:
A poster frame is a representative frame of the video: the picture of the asset's thumbnail in the browser and the rundown, and the frame other systems can use (for example, a Video-on-Demand archive).

  • How to set: Navigate to the desired frame in the player timeline, then click the Set poster frame button on the toolbar. The asset's thumbnail changes to the new frame.

docs.title: Trimming
docs.text:
Trimming allows you to define custom playback start and end points for an asset without altering the source file: 1. Seek to the desired start point and set the IN mark. 2. Seek to the desired end point and set the OUT mark. 3. Click Save Marks.

When you drag the asset onto a playlist, only the region between the IN and OUT marks will be played. VOD transcoders also respect these marks to crop output files.

docs.title: Sub-clips
docs.text:
Sub-clips allow you to non-destructively split a single parent media asset into multiple child clips (e.g. news segments, individual songs from a concert video). Sub-clips can overlap.

  • Create Sub-clip: Set your IN and OUT marks, then click Create sub-clip in the toolbar.
  • Manage Sub-clips: Rename, modify, or delete existing segments by clicking Manage sub-clips.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The player interface keyboard shortcuts are derived from standard non-linear editors (like Avid Media Composer or Adobe Premiere), ensuring a familiar layout for video editors:

Shortcut Action / Description 1 or J Seek backward 5 frames 2 or L Seek forward 5 frames 3 or Left Seek backward 1 frame (fine tuning) 4 or Right Seek forward 1 frame (fine tuning) A or Home Seek to the beginning of the file S or End Seek to the end of the file Q Go directly to the IN mark W Go directly to the OUT mark E or I Set IN mark R or O Set OUT mark D Clear the IN mark F Clear the OUT mark Space or K Toggle Play / Pause
